content: The design and implementation of an HIV case surveillance system must be tailored to the specific context of each country. In nations with a robust disease-reporting framework that does not yet include HIV, mechanisms for establishing HIV case surveillance may already exist. These mechanisms likely include methods for adding HIV to the list of reportable diseases, identifying responsible agencies for oversight, defining reporting pathways, and assigning individuals responsible for reporting. In such cases, the focus of implementation will be on HIV-specific factors, such as case definitions, reporting timeframes, case report forms, sentinel events, data sources, methods for identifying and reporting cases, data management systems, analysis and dissemination, security and confidentiality, performance standards, required resources, and training. In countries with limited or non-existent disease case reporting systems, the implementation process may involve multiple steps. The outlined approach is designed to guide countries lacking a strong disease surveillance system, particularly one that is case-based. These strategies can also be applied to countries seeking to strengthen their existing HIV surveillance systems. The Ministry of Health should lead the development and implementation of HIV case surveillance, with input from relevant stakeholders. Ideally, a steering committee should be established, comprising organizations and agencies involved in and benefiting from the surveillance program. This may include representatives from the national Ministry of Health, HIV testing and treatment programs, laboratories conducting HIV-related tests, national statistical and vital registration agencies, monitoring and evaluation staff, health management information systems, planning bodies, community organizations, implementing partners, policymakers, and donors. Training and capacity building are essential, as are clearly defined roles and responsibilities, stakeholder engagement, governance, leadership, and a regulatory framework. Effective management and supervision, adequate human resources, and reliable data sources are critical. Sentinel events, data elements, data submission processes, and case surveillance databases must be established. Data transfer, quality assurance, and case-matching methods should be implemented, along with robust data systems and management practices. Data analysis, system monitoring, quality improvement, and data utilization are key components of a successful surveillance system. A situational assessment is necessary to design a surveillance system that aligns with the environment in which cases can be identified and reported. This assessment should include a review of existing documents, field visits to facilities and laboratories, and consultations with health facilities and community-based organizations involved in HIV testing and care. The assessment should evaluate existing HIV reporting laws and regulations, patient privacy and data security policies, organizational structures for disease surveillance, reporting pathways, data management systems, and dissemination processes. It should also identify data collection tools, data gaps, weaknesses in the surveillance system, and the potential for leveraging electronic medical records (EMRs) and laboratory information systems. Additionally, the assessment should examine the completeness of vital registration systems, technological capacity, infrastructure, and the availability of human and financial resources. Countries should set clear objectives for implementing or upgrading their HIV case surveillance systems. These objectives may include measuring the number and trends of HIV cases, demographic information, modes of transmission, entry into care, time from diagnosis to care, clinical characteristics at diagnosis, initiation and retention on antiretroviral therapy (ART), changes in clinical staging and immunological status, time to viral suppression, and mortality. Other objectives may involve measuring disease burden by transmission mode and geography, identifying outbreaks or hotspots, assessing the impact of prevention and care efforts, and using data for program improvement and resource allocation. The surveillance system design should incorporate all reporting processes and procedures, informed by the situational analysis. The implementation plan must define which Ministry of Health programs will oversee the system, manage data, analyze and disseminate information, and monitor system performance. Reporting pathways should be established, considering whether reports should first be submitted at the subnational level or directly to the national level. The system should, at a minimum, describe the magnitude and direction of the epidemic and measure strategic information indicators for HIV by sex, age, geography, transmission mode, and time. Case report forms should be user-friendly, include instructions for completion and submission, and provide contact information for questions. In settings without a unique patient identifier, guidance on introducing a national health identifier may be necessary. Methods for electronic data transfer from EMRs, registers, and laboratory systems to the surveillance program should be developed by information technologists and data managers. Electronic reporting should only be considered in settings with stable power sources and appropriate IT infrastructure. Countries should avoid adopting new technology without adequate support. Key principles for data management systems include accessibility for authorized personnel, modifiable software, local IT support, simplicity, de-duplication capabilities, security protections, automated and manual data quality checks, and compliance with national laws governing public health data. The system should support data transfer between subnational and national levels, ensure compatibility with case report forms, and include interoperability for electronic uploads. Data standards, a data dictionary, and skilled personnel or commercial suppliers are essential. Surveillance policies, processes, and data systems must adhere to national or international standards for patient privacy and data security. Confidentiality and security must be prioritized at every step of system design. For example, secure methods must be developed for transporting case reports to the surveillance program. The system should be designed to achieve recommended performance standards, such as completeness, timeliness, and accuracy of case surveillance. Reporting from laboratories enhances case ascertainment and laboratory variable completeness. Human and financial resources must also be considered in system design. A technical guidance document should record national regulations, laws, policies, and procedures for HIV case surveillance. This document, also known as an operations manual, should be available at national and subnational levels. It should include a glossary of terms, the purpose of the document and surveillance, national reporting mandates, case definitions, reporting pathways, required variables, data transmission procedures, hardware and software descriptions, dissemination plans, monitoring processes, security requirements, roles and responsibilities, training requirements, and key contacts. Pilot testing may be useful in settings where implementation methods are not well-defined. This allows for system modifications before national rollout. Pilot testing should be conducted in selected regions or sites, planned for a specific time period, and include an evaluation protocol to measure performance standards and other system attributes. Following the pilot, the system can be rolled out nationally or expanded further.
